pages.text:
6:47 a.m. Saturday. The roar hit me before my eyes were open.

"RAAAAWR," said Gus, his face a green blur of spikes and fury.

I did not wait for him to finish. I looked at the ceiling, where a pale rectangle marked where my poster used to be, and I said, "I choose it."

The word felt heavy in my mouth. Like a rock I had just picked up from the sidewalk.

"On purpose," I added. "Before anything happens."

I felt stupid. I felt like an eleven-year-old trying to do algebra. But I said it again, quieter this time. "I choose it."

Then I looked down at Gus. He was vibrating with energy, ready to start the day’s chaos. I took a breath. I filled my lungs with the stale, box-dust air of my room. And I let it out.

"RAAAAWWWRRR!"

I did it at maximum volume. I put my whole chest into it. It was ugly. It was loud. It was the most honest thing I had done in seventy-two Saturdays.

Gus froze. His mouth stopped moving. A smile, tiny and white, cracked across his face inside the hood. He slid off my chest and landed on the floor with a thud, giggling.

I lay there, panting, staring at the ceiling. I had chosen this. And it was not so bad.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, lies in bed shouting loudly while Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, sits on the floor laughing with his mouth wide open; morning light, bare room.

pages.text:
7:13 a.m. Waffles trotted past my door with my left slipper hanging out of his mouth like a cigar.

In seventy-two Saturdays, I had chased him. In seventy-two Saturdays, I had snatched it back. Today, I just watched him go.

He disappeared under the dining room table, and I could hear the soft, rhythmic crunch of him chewing. I crawled after him, a move I had never attempted before. Underneath was a cave, dark and cool, smelling like old carpet and warm dog breath.

I found the usual suspects: one lost sock, one red Lego brick, and the fossilized french fry that had been there since the Clinton administration. Waffles lay in the middle of them, looking pleased with himself.

I didn't grab the slipper. Instead, I reached behind me and pulled off my right one. I held it out into the shadows.

Waffles looked at the slipper. Then he looked at me. He gave a low, rumbling bark, which I decided was a yes. I slid the second slipper under the table to him.

He nudged it closer to his paws. We lay there, me in my boxers and him with two slippers. Dust motes danced in the thin beam of light from the hallway. It was quiet. It was peaceful. For the first time, I was not waiting for the day to start. I was just being in it.

Waffles rested his white front paw on my ankle. I did not move.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in boxers, lies on the floor under a dining table next to Waffles, a chubby corgi holding two slippers; dusty light beams, a lost sock and a french fry visible.

pages.text:
7:22 a.m. The smoke alarm screamed, and Dad was already on his chair, fanning the air with a dish towel.

"Max! Good morning! Did you know I'm reading a book about anti-gravity?"

I walked over to the toaster. The toast was black, the exact color of a tire. In previous Saturdays, I would have groaned. Today, I took a slice and scraped the charcoal off into the sink. It made a gritty sound, like sand in my teeth.

I spread thick, sweet peanut butter on it and took a bite.

It was crisp and salty and the best thing I had ever tasted. I ate the whole slice standing right there in the kitchen.

Dad watched me. His mustache twitched. "It's impossible to put down!"

I looked at him. I really looked at him. His eyes were bright, and he was waiting.

I laughed until my ribs hurt. It was a real laugh, the kind that comes from your belly, not your throat.

Dad’s face lit up. He looked like he had won the lottery. He got down off the chair and gave me a hug that smelled like smoke and breakfast. I hugged back. I felt something loose in my chest, a knot that had been there for weeks, finally give way.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, laughs while eating toast next to Dad, a big man in a fish apron standing on a chair; smoke alarm beeping, kitchen with boxes.

pages.text:
At 8:05, Mrs. Abernathy stood at the door, balancing a casserole dish that looked too heavy for her hands.

"It's a hot dish," she said, her voice thin and polite. "So be careful. You'll want a trivet."

In seventy-two Saturdays, I had ignored her. Today, I stepped into her space. "Thank you, Mrs. Abernathy. Can I ask you something?"

She blinked, her eyes kind but tired. "Yes, caro."

"Why do you bring one every Saturday?"

She didn't answer right away. Instead, she looked at the casserole, then at the house, then at the boxes stacked in the hallway.

"When you lose someone," she said softly, "you still cook. Your hands know what to do. I cook for the street because it is how I say I care."

She stepped back, but I moved forward instead. I wrapped my arms around her, feeling her small and solid frame against my chest. She smelled of tomato leaves and lavender, like a garden that had been left alone for a week. I held on tight, and she held on back.

"I am glad you are here," I whispered.

She patted my head. "I am glad you are eating."
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy, hugs Mrs. Abernathy, an 80s-year-old woman in a floral hat, in a hallway filled with moving boxes; warm, emotional mood, soft light.

pages.text:
By noon, I had to admit the truth to myself.

The day hadn't changed, and the toast was still charcoal, and the box had still hit the floor, so nothing outside had moved which meant I was the only variable left in the equation.

I went to my room where the walls were bare, but on the inside of my closet door my tally marks waited, seventy-two loops of survival scratched in pencil.

I took out my pencil and didn't add a new mark, but I wrote one line, small and neat, just below the scratches.

THE DAY IS THE SAME. I DON'T HAVE TO BE.

I stared at it, and it felt true, like a backpack that had finally dropped a heavy dictionary.

Then I heard the slam.

A crash followed, the garage door banging against the frame hard enough to rattle the window glass in its track, and Tessa was in there tapping her drumsticks on the metal in a sharp, angry rhythm that sounded like a countdown.

My knees went weak because I had chosen happiness, and I had chosen peace, and now the day was reminding me that I was still eleven and still moving to a place that was mostly cactus.

I walked toward the garage, not to fix it, but just to be there.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy, stands in a hallway looking at a closed garage door; moving boxes in the background, a sense of tension and anticipation.
